When instantiating a 'Star' mobject, use the keyword argument 'n' to specify the number of points; do not use 'n_outer' or 'n_points'.
When presenting two mobjects for comparison (e.g., prediction vs ground truth), assign them to the same grid row or column to maintain logical alignment for the viewer.
To rotate a mobject between grid points, calculate the angle using 'angle_of_vector(self.grid[target] - self.grid[source])'; do not use the 'Angle' class with numpy arrays.

To prevent render timeouts, instantiate persistent mobjects (including `SVGMobject`) during setup rather than inside frame-by-frame updaters like `always_redraw`; use `add_updater` with direct property manipulation (e.g., `mobject.move_to`) to update the existing instance.
Use the 'Indicate' animation class to emphasize a mobject; avoid using 'Indication', as it is not a valid class name and will trigger a NameError.

Align the grid row of supplemental mobjects (equations/labels) with the vertical position of the lecture bullet point they describe to maintain logical synchronization.
Position sequential mobjects (icons followed by formulas) in adjacent grid rows without empty intermediate rows to maintain visual conceptual grouping.

Topic: Abstract Vector Spaces: Beyond the Arrow

Target audience: University undergraduate students (STEM)

Section: section_1 — The Starting Point: Familiar Euclidean Space

Lecture lines:
Vectors are often pictured as arrows in space.
We add them by placing them tip-to-tail.
We scale them by stretching or shrinking.
These operations define the geometry of R-squared.
But vectors are much more than just arrows.

Planned animations:
A 2D coordinate grid appears with a green vector arrow #00FF00 starting at the origin.
A blue vector #00BFFF is added to the first, showing the parallelogram addition rule.
The green vector scales to double its length to demonstrate scalar multiplication.

Section: section_2 — The 'What If' Moment: Generalization

Lecture lines:
Can other objects behave like these arrows?
Consider functions that we add and scale.
Vector spaces are broader than we often imagine.

Planned animations:
The 2D grid and arrows fade out to a black background.
Icons for a 2x2 matrix, a function curve, and a sequence appear in the center. #F08080
A white boundary #FFFFFF surrounds the icons, labeled as a 'Vector Space V'.

Section: section_3 — The 8 Axioms: The 'Membership Rules'

Lecture lines:
A vector space follows eight strict rules.
These axioms ensure consistent addition and scaling.
Every space must contain a zero element.
Every element must have an additive inverse.
Passing these tests defines a vector space.

Planned animations:
The Commutativity axiom 'u + v = v + u' appears in light blue #ADD8E6 at the top.
The Associativity axiom '(u + v) + w = u + (v + w)' appears below it.
The Additive Identity axiom 'v + 0 = v' appears on the right side.
The Distributive property 'a(u + v) = au + av' appears below the identity.
All displayed axioms flash and turn light green #90EE90 to show they define the space.

Section: section_4 — Abstract Example: The Space of Polynomials

Lecture lines:
Consider the set of all low-degree polynomials.
Adding two polynomials results in another polynomial.
We can even visualize coefficients as coordinates.

Planned animations:
A polynomial 'P(x) = ax^2 + bx + c' appears in gold #FFD700.
A second polynomial 'Q(x) = dx^2 + ex + f' appears below it.
The coefficients of P and Q group together to show how polynomials add like vectors.
A scalar 'k' multiplies each term of P(x), changing its color to cyan #00FFFF.
A label 'Polynomial Space' appears at the bottom in orange #FFA500.

Section: section_5 — The Power of Abstraction: Why It Matters

Lecture lines:
Abstraction lets us solve many problems at once.
One theorem applies to arrows and functions.
Digital signals are processed as abstract vectors.
This 'Master Key' simplifies complex mathematical systems.
We look past form to see underlying structure.

Planned animations:
Three icons representing 'Physics', 'AI', and 'Signals' appear in purple #DDA0DD.
Arrows from each icon point toward a central 'Vector Space' circle. #FFFFFF
The central circle pulses with a pale yellow light #FFFFE0 to signify universal application.

Section: section_6 — Summary and Conclusion

Lecture lines:
Vectors are elements of any valid vector space.
We moved from arrows to abstract rules.
Linear algebra reveals these universal mathematical patterns.

Planned animations:
A vector arrow and a polynomial equation appear side-by-side in white #FFFFFF.
A green frame #00FF00 labeled '8 Axioms' wraps around both objects.
All elements fade out, leaving the final title 'Abstract Vector Spaces' in white.
